articles.title: How to beat the fine print

body.support:
Gyms, phone plans and games all have **terms and conditions**. When you tick *I agree*, it's a **contract**. You have to keep it.

You don't need to read every word. Here's how.

**1. Skim the headings.** Look for *Fees*, *Cancel* and *Changes*.

**2. Scan for $.** Look for words like *fee*, *cancel* and *renew*.

**3. Read those parts.** Find:

- the **real cost** ($19.95 a fortnight is $518.70 a year!)
- the **minimum term**: how long you're stuck
- **auto-renew**: does it keep charging you?
- the **cancellation fee**

**4. Must or may?** *Must* means someone **has to**. *May* means they're **allowed to**. *We may change our fees.*

**5. Say it in plain words.** *Termination of membership* means *cancelling*.

**6. Keep a copy.** Take a screenshot.
body.core:
Gyms, phone plans, streaming services, games, concert tickets: they all come with **terms and conditions**. When you tick *I agree*, you're agreeing to a **contract**. You have to keep it.

The fine print is long on purpose. You don't need to read every word. You need a plan.

**1. Skim the headings.** Terms and conditions are split into sections with headings, like *Fees*, *Term*, *Cancellation* and *Changes*. These show you where the important parts are.

**2. Scan for money and key words.** Look for **$**, and words like *fee*, *cancel*, *renew* and *minimum*. These are the parts that can cost you.

**3. Read those parts closely.** Look for:

- the **real cost**: $19.95 a fortnight is $518.70 a year
- the **minimum term**: how long you're locked in
- **auto-renew**: does it keep charging you until you cancel?
- the **cancellation fee**, and how you have to cancel
- what they're allowed to **change**

**4. Watch the small words.** *Must* means someone **has to**: *You must give 30 days' notice.* *May* means someone is **allowed to**, if they choose: *We may change our fees.* Notice who has to, and who gets to choose.

**5. Unpack the legal language.** Contracts often turn actions into nouns. *Termination of membership requires the provision of written notice* just means: *To cancel, tell us in writing.* Rewrite it in plain English.

**6. Keep a copy.** Screenshot the terms, and set a reminder before anything renews.

The law protects you too. Since **November 2023**, businesses in Australia can be fined for using **unfair terms** in standard contracts. And a business must not mislead you about your choices.
body.extend:
Gym memberships, phone plans, streaming services, games and tickets all come with **terms and conditions**. Accepting them creates a **contract**: a legally binding agreement.

The length and density of fine print discourage reading. Rather than reading every word, read strategically.

**1. Skim the structure.** Terms are organised into sections with headings, such as *Fees*, *Term*, *Cancellation* and *Variations*. The structure shows where the consequential content sits.

**2. Scan for cost and commitment.** Search for **$** and key terms: *fee*, *cancel*, *renew*, *minimum*, *variation*.

**3. Read closely.** Establish:

- the **true cost** (annualise it: $19.95 a fortnight is $518.70 a year)
- the **minimum term**
- whether it **auto-renews**
- the **cancellation fee** and process
- what the business may **vary**

**4. Read the modal verbs.** *Must* creates an **obligation**: *You must give 30 days' notice.* *May* grants a **discretion**: *We may vary our fees.* Mapping who must and who may shows where power sits in the contract.

**5. Unpack nominalisation.** Legal writing often turns actions into nouns, which hides who does what. *Termination of membership requires the provision of written notice* becomes *To cancel, you must tell us in writing.*

**6. Keep records.** Save a copy and note renewal dates.

Since **9 November 2023**, businesses that use **unfair terms** in standard form contracts can face penalties. The Australian Consumer Law also bans misleading conduct, including about consumers' options.

caseStudies.title: The choice that was hard to find

body.support:
Microsoft 365 is a subscription for apps like Word. Lots of students use it.

In **2024**, Microsoft added an AI helper, **Copilot**, and raised the price. The Personal plan went from **$109 to $159** a year.

In **2025**, the **ACCC** took Microsoft to court. The ACCC protects shoppers. It says people were told: pay more, or cancel.

But the ACCC says there was a **third choice**. A **Classic** plan, with no Copilot, at the old price. You only saw it if you started to **cancel**.

Microsoft said sorry and offered refunds.

The court will decide if Microsoft broke the law. The lesson: look for the choices they don't show you.
body.core:
Microsoft 365 is a subscription for apps like Word and Excel. Many students and families use it.

In late **2024**, Microsoft added its AI helper, **Copilot**, to its Personal and Family plans. It also raised the price. The yearly price of the **Personal** plan went from **$109 to $159**. The **Family** plan went from **$139 to $179**.

In **October 2025**, the **ACCC**, the government agency that protects consumers, took Microsoft to court. About **2.7 million** Australians had plans that **auto-renew**. The ACCC says they were told they had two choices: pay the new, higher price, or cancel.

But the ACCC says there was a **third choice**: a **Classic** plan, with no Copilot, at the old price. The ACCC alleges Microsoft didn't mention it in its emails. The only way to find it was to **start cancelling** your subscription.

In **November 2025**, Microsoft said sorry to Australian subscribers. It said it could have been clearer. It offered refunds to people who switched to the Classic plan.

The court will decide if Microsoft broke the law. But the lesson for every subscriber is the same: read what you're agreeing to, and look for the choices they don't put on the front page.
body.extend:
Microsoft 365 is an app subscription widely used by students and families.

From late **2024**, Microsoft added its AI assistant, **Copilot**, to its Personal and Family plans and raised prices. The yearly **Personal** plan rose **45%**, from **$109 to $159**. The **Family** plan rose from **$139 to $179**.

In **October 2025**, the **ACCC** took Microsoft to the Federal Court. It alleges that about **2.7 million** Australian subscribers on auto-renewal were told they had two options: accept Copilot at the higher price, or cancel. The ACCC says there was a third option it didn't mention: a **Classic** plan without Copilot, at the old price. Subscribers could only reach it by starting to cancel.

In **November 2025**, Microsoft publicly apologised to Australian subscribers. It said it could have been clearer about the options, and offered refunds to those who switched to Classic.

These are allegations, and the court will decide them. But the case shows how the way choices are presented can steer people. That's why it pays to read past the headline message.

teacher.overview: The boss level of Money Moves. Students learn to read terms and conditions strategically: skimming headings, scanning for cost and commitment, and reading key sections closely. Language focus: technical terms (minimum term, auto-renew, cancellation fee, direct debit), modal verbs of obligation and possibility (must, may) and who holds them, and nominalisation in legal writing, unpacked into plain English. The case study is the ACCC's 2025 Federal Court case alleging Microsoft didn't tell subscribers about a cheaper plan. The final task reads real terms and summarises them in plain English for a friend.
prep: Collect 3–4 sets of real terms and conditions students might meet: a gym, a phone plan, a streaming service, a game or a ticketing site. Print the key sections if devices are limited.
Check those pages are reachable on school devices.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** the real cost, minimum term, auto-renewal, the cancellation fee and process, what they may change. Must = someone has to; may = someone is allowed to. So you can prove what you agreed to, and check renewal dates.

**Terms:** 1 fees ($518.70 a year + $49); 2 minimum term (12 months); 3 auto-renew; 4 cancelling (nominalised: tell us in writing 30 days before); 5 early exit fee ($199); 6 may (they can raise fees); 7 must (you have to keep details up to date).

**Sort:** 30 days' notice — must, you; change fees — may, business; payment details — must, you; suspend service — may, business; be 18 — must, you; change content — may, business.

**Unpack it (samples):** if you don't pay, we'll stop you getting in; if you cancel before 12 months, you'll pay $199; your subscription renews automatically; we can change our fees if we tell you 30 days before.

**Cost:** 26 × $19.95 = $518.70 + $49 = $567.70. Six months: 13 × $19.95 = $259.35 + $49 + $199 = $507.35, almost as much as a whole year.

**Case study:** accept Copilot at a higher price, or cancel; a Classic plan without Copilot at the old price, reached only by starting to cancel; an allegation is a claim not yet proven in court, so we report it as what the ACCC says.

realityCheck: **Check the case before teaching it.** The Microsoft case was before the Federal Court when this course was written. Search the ACCC's media releases for an outcome, and teach the difference between an allegation and a finding.
**Real terms are very long.** Print only the key sections (fees, term, cancellation, changes) for weaker readers; the skill is finding them.
**Students already have contracts:** phone plans, game subscriptions, streaming. Some will find something they want to cancel. Let them.
**Under-18s and contracts.** Many services need a parent or an over-18 account holder. Students still need the skill, and often explain terms to their families.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It's the natural finale to Money Moves, using payslip, budget and shopping skills together.
